claim: Problem and solution are developed in parallel and bridged: in a protocol study of 9 professional designers, creative moments coincided with a bridge where a problem frame and a partial solution fit each other.
agent_test: Compare an S2-S3 loop that may revise the problem frame after a solution attempt against a frame-once-then-solve run, at equal tokens, on open-ended design tasks.

claim: Co-evolution is seen across several independent qualitative and protocol studies (teams, experts, students, ethnography), but each is small and descriptive; no study tests it against a rival model.
agent_test: Log how often the agent's frame changes after a solution step; check whether frame changes track final score.
audit_note: Opened Parsons, PMC ethnography, Feast, Hu, Storm and Maher-Tang abstract pages; all small qualitative or protocol studies as described. Absence claim (no rival-model test) not testable from sources, and Cash et al. 2023 is a quantitative reanalysis but not a rival-model test.

claim: Co-evolution of problem and solution is widely treated as a valid model of design (Cross: general validity confirmed in nine-designer protocol data), but its direction is not fixed (the solution space may be structured before the problem space), and Halstrom and Galle argue it leaves practitioners without guidance; the claim that it is not defining or does not always occur is not shown in the sources opened.
agent_test: Allow zero reframes; compare an always-reframe forced loop with an optional one.
audit_note: The Halstrom and Galle abstract only says co-evolution has merit but leaves practitioners without guidance; the full-text statement that it is not defining and does not always occur could not be retrieved (PDF download truncated twice); Cross's chapter says the model's general validity is confirmed, with direction not fixed.
claim_before_audit: Co-evolution is common but not defining or universal; it does not always occur, even in non-trivial cases.

claim: In a qualitative study of 11 expert visualization designers (Parsons and Shukla 2025), reframing was often prompted by solution-side events such as tool limits, time pressure and abandoned chart designs that failed to convey the message, not only by a planned problem-framing step; a quantitative protocol study of student teams found this only overall and reversed during ideation.
agent_test: Trigger frame revision only on a failed or surprising solution check; compare with revision at fixed intervals.
audit_note: Only Parsons and Shukla (n=11, qualitative vignettes) opened and it supports solution-side triggers (tool limits, time pressure, abandoned chart designs); the second listed source (Applied Sciences 2020) returned Access Denied, its evidence lines show new problem entities followed solution work only overall and reversed in ideation, and Parsons is listed twice; Cash et al. 2023 links transitions to uncertainty, not solution-side events. 'Mostly' is not shown by any quantified count.
claim_before_audit: Reframing is triggered mostly by solution-side events (failed attempts, tool limits, a chart that fails to show patterns), not by a planned problem step.

claim: The textbook mapping analysis=problem space, synthesis=solution space fails: analysis correlated negatively with problem-related transitions (rS=-0.649), only evaluation matched solution space (rS=0.672); 24 fragments from 4 teams of 3.
agent_test: Do not tie operators to spaces by name; tag each agent step by content (problem entity vs solution entity) and check.

claim: In team protocols, new problem entities appear more often right after solution-space work than after problem-space work overall; the pattern reverses within ideation alone.
agent_test: Count new constraints found after solution steps in agent traces.

claim: Time spent structuring the problem is linked to better creative outcomes in human design (Christiaans, Akin and Akin, Atman, Kokotovich 2008), but these were second-hand or from memory, correlational, and the numbers were not read here. Re-check: the 2008 Kokotovich paper is closed access; the abstract and the author's own 2015 summary show within-group correlations in one student mind-map study, with no numbers. Kruger and Cross 2006 (N=9, abstract only) says solution-driven designers scored higher on creativity and lower on quality, and problem-driven designers balanced both.
agent_test: Compare short vs long problem-mapping before generation at equal total tokens.

claim: Muddling through (solution-first, reflective) versus problem-first is an open dispute: Kokotovich argues forestalling solutions helps; Cross (2024) adds that in creative design the solution space may be structured first from precedents; Kruger and Cross (2006) compared strategies (not read).
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: problem-first, solution-first, interleaved; score novelty and correctness.

claim: Students split into problem-driven and solution-driven by FBS P-S index (N=54) show different cognitive processes; outcome-quality effect not read.
agent_test: Use as a classification idea for agent traces.

claim: LLM reframing help: a randomized test (280 frames rated by 15 experts, 4 arms) found no gain in novelty or usefulness of problem frames from GPT-4o, in direct, Dorst-structured or free-form use.
agent_test: Replicate with a model-run frame step vs none, blind judged, equal tokens.

claim: The structured Dorst nine-step chain took about 22% more time (28.35 vs 23.25 min) and gave no quality gain; users felt supported (CSI about 61-65) regardless of arm.
agent_test: Treat long reframing chains as a cost that must earn a held-out gain; felt help is not evidence.

claim: LLM reframing helps skilled users more than novices (12.54% more novel frames, z=2.70, p=0.01); the free-form gap of 20.84% was not significant.
agent_test: Not an agent test; shows outcome depends on who steers.

claim: A small study (N=7) found a 4-call Dorst-style chain rated more interesting (29/189 vs 17/189); it measures interest, not expert-rated quality, and it is problem-first, so it is not a test of co-evolution.
agent_test: Use expert or ground-truth scoring.

claim: Restating the problem before solving raises LLM accuracy when wording is ambiguous: GPT-4 average over 10 tasks 64.95 to 89.77 with Rephrase-and-Respond; smaller models gain less and sometimes lose. Vicuna-13b answering its own rephrase scored lower than answering GPT-4's rephrase on all 6 tasks tried (e.g. Sports 65.00 vs 73.64).
agent_test: Test restate-then-solve vs solve at equal tokens; include a weak model.

claim: Asking for the underlying principle first (step-back) raised PaLM-2L on MMLU physics 66.4 to 73.2 and chemistry 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66; it fixes up to 40% of errors and adds up to 12% new ones.
agent_test: Compare with and without a step-back call at equal tokens; report new errors introduced.
audit_note: All step-back numbers match Zheng et al. (66.4 to 73.2, 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66, errors fixed up to ~40% and new errors max ~12%); the second listed source (Self-Discover) is a different method and does not corroborate, so the claim rests on one paper (Google, no independent replication).

claim: Pre-solving frame steps help in several checkable-answer LLM tasks (RaR, step-back, Self-Discover) yet were null for open-ended design problem frames (Shin) and for a reframe-as-HMW prompt (IDEAFix): benefit appears where the answer is checkable.
agent_test: Run the same frame step on checkable and open-ended items and compare.

claim: In one 48-hour hackathon (Egea et al. 2024) a ChatGPT-4-led team placed second of six but abandoned promising concepts after minor difficulties, added needless complexity and showed design fixation; an unreviewed preprint (O'Hara) reports that LLM assistants tend to accept a user's technology choice without validating requirements and proposes a Five Whys workflow, whose reported detection rate and cost could not be checked.
agent_test: Seed items with a wrong stated premise; measure how often the agent checks it.
audit_note: Hackathon result matches Egea et al. (second of six, abandoned concepts on minor difficulties, fixation); for O'Hara only the abstract-level solution-jumping description was reachable (techrxiv blocked), so the 100% detection of 6 seeded mismatches and about 0.01 USD per session could not be verified, and 'LLMs jump to solutions' generalizes from one self-evaluated preprint and one hackathon.
claim_before_audit: LLMs jump to solutions: they accept a user's tool choice without checking requirements; in a hackathon a ChatGPT-led team dropped good concepts after small snags and fixated; a Five Whys workflow detected 100% of 6 seeded mismatches at about 0.01 USD per session.

claim: Models solve fully specified problems but fail to ask for the one missing piece: QuestBench best models above 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but only 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q.
agent_test: Add an 'is anything missing' check; measure on QuestBench-like items.

claim: Asking clarifying questions before coding raised GPT-4 Pass@1 from 70.96 to 80.80 on MBPP-sanitized with human answers (10 participants, 140 problems), and about 10-13 points with simulated users over four benchmarks.
agent_test: Clarify-then-solve vs solve at equal tokens with a simulated answerer; count extra-call cost.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A second agent that monitors progress gave better designs than a plain retry loop: battery capacity 141.17 Ah vs 72.07 plain vs 106.08 self-monitor, 30 runs each, F(2,86)=21.606, d=1.85. All three arms stopped after about 9 steps on average (9.07 / 9.10 / 9.37, F(2,87)=0.031, p=.97), so steps are equal, but monitor calls add tokens that were not measured; one task, one model.
agent_test: Rerun at equal total tokens including the monitor, on several tasks and models.

claim: In human design with generative AI, AI groups got higher problem-framing and mechanism-breadth ratings (dz about 2.5) but lower innovation (4.66 vs 3.40, dz 2.69); a Double Diamond structure beat GAI alone, but the reported F is inconsistent (see critique).
agent_test: Check whether breadth up and innovation down also holds for agent output: score both.

claim: LLM output stays in one semantic region despite defixation prompts or framing (pairwise cosine novelty distances 0.206-0.341); framing the brief measurably changes novelty and diversity.
agent_test: Measure embedding spread under frame changes at equal tokens.

claim: Full text read: GPT-4o told to act as problem-driven or solution-driven designer matched human static issue shares but not transitions. The problem-driven persona made fewer problem-solution switches (PS 6.7 vs 10.5, SP 6.4 vs 9.8, p<=.003 unconstrained) than the solution-driven one; both beat a bare prompt on novelty and integrity (p<.05). 10 runs per cell, one model, one task, no test that transition complexity predicts quality.
agent_test: Force at least one return from solution to problem in the scaffold and code the trace; do not rely on a persona prompt.

claim: Co-evolving loops degrade without a bound: R-Zero gained +5.51 math points over three iterations while pseudo-label accuracy fell from 79.0 to 63.0 percent, and the smallest model peaked at step 15 (larger models declined later); the Microsoft theory-loop (Comet-H) design includes a grounding ledger, a half-life on carried follow-ups and re-checks of claims against code, but the paper only predicts, and does not test, what removing them would cause.
agent_test: Cap reframe rounds; test 0, 1, 2, 3 rounds at equal tokens.
audit_note: R-Zero numbers verified (+5.51 math, pseudo-label accuracy 79.0 to 63.0 over three iterations, smallest 0.6B peaks at step 15 while the 4B model declines only at step 60), but in Young and Bjorner the ledger, follow-up half-life and re-checks are described as design choices whose removal effects are only predicted (Table 7), not shown to be needed.
claim_before_audit: Co-evolving loops need a bound: R-Zero gained +5.51 math points but pseudo-label accuracy fell 79.0 to 63.0 percent in 3 iterations and small models declined after about step 15; the Microsoft theory loop needed a ledger, follow-up decay and re-checks.

claim: No published LLM study tests problem-first against co-evolving order with numbers. One full-text LLM study codes transitions (Zhang 2025, 10 runs per cell) and finds LLM traces make fewer cross-space switches than humans; none tests whether transition complexity predicts quality.
agent_test: This is the open experiment for our agent.

claim: Co-evolution as a computational model (Maher and Poon) lets requirements and solutions change together in a genetic algorithm; abstracts give no human-fit data.
agent_test: Let a failed S3 rewrite the S2 criteria; compare with fixed criteria.

claim: Expert frame work alternates between exploring and committing; experience changes the reasoning mode (12 experts, three modes). Qualitative only.
agent_test: Description only.

claim: Failed-check or concrete-symptom triggers beat generic reflection at equal budget: symptom-triggered intervention repaired 20.15% of 536 failed agent runs vs 6.90% for unguided rerun, 4.29% self-reflection, 3.73% critic and random-node. Not a frame-revision task.
agent_test: Gate the return on an external failed check; include a resample-only arm at equal tokens.

claim: Self-judged correction loops degrade: with no outside signal, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell 75.8 to 38.1 after one round and GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two; an oracle trigger gained (GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5). Voting beat debate at equal responses.
agent_test: Limit reframes to 2 or 3 and only on a verified failure; keep best-so-far.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Iterative refinement with clear feedback gains most in rounds 1-3 and is sometimes non-monotonic (code optimisation 22.0 to 28.8 after 3 rounds; max 4).
agent_test: Default cap 2-3 rounds.

claim: Segment-level protocol data link co-evolution moves to uncertainty: in 1617 segments from 31 novices, hedging level differed by transition type (chi2(6)=180.1) and marked transition changes (t=-3.905), but pseudo R2 was about 1% and change in hedging was not significant (p=.117).
agent_test: Use solution-side uncertainty as a soft trigger together with a check.

claim: Human order comparison on outcomes is thin: Kruger and Cross 2006 (N=9, abstract only) reports solution-driven = higher creativity, lower quality; problem-driven = best balance. Kokotovich 2008 is correlational and closed. No direct problem-first vs solution-first vs interleaved experiment with numbers was found.
agent_test: Run the three orders at equal tokens on one open-ended and one checkable task set.

claim: Dorst and Cross 2001 remains N=9, one task; full text not reached, no replication on the original expert data found. The nearest quantitative support is Cash et al. 2023 (31 novices, 1617 segments).
agent_test: Treat as a descriptive model, not an effect size.

claim: Clarification steps are fragile even on checkable tasks: Lean spec generation with clarification went -2.6 pp (same-model, 189 tasks) to +6.3 pp (cross-model), k=10 no better than k=3; detecting under-specification is easier than using the answer.
agent_test: Cap questions at about 3; test the use step; expect weaker transfer to open-ended design.

claim: Model tier and user skill moderate frame steps: self-rephrase helped GPT-4 but sometimes hurt GPT-3.5 and Vicuna, while a stronger model's rephrase lifted Vicuna on 6 of 6 tasks; skilled users got 12.54% more novel frames (p=.01). A schema should gate self-framing by model tier or use a stronger framer.
agent_test: Compare self-frame, stronger-model frame and no frame on weak and strong models at equal tokens.
